opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends on where you believe your unfair advantage actually lies, and most teams get this wrong by trying to build everything.

If you're pursuing something as ambitious as physical AGI, the core bet is usually on the intelligence: the learning algorithms, the data engine, the way you scale up experience. That's the part you have to own. If you outsource your data pipeline or your model training stack, you've basically outsourced your thesis. So I'd say build anything that sits on the critical path of your learning loop: how you collect data, how you curate it, how fast you can go from a failure in the real world to an improved policy. Iteration speed there is everything.

Hardware is where it gets tricky. There's a romantic notion that you need to build your own robot from the ground up, and sometimes that's true. If your approach depends on a form factor, sensing modality, or cost point that doesn't exist on the market, you may have no choice. But hardware is a deep, unforgiving discipline. Supply chains, reliability, maintenance, all of that eats engineering bandwidth that could go into the learning problem. A lot of early teams, including academic labs, have burned years building hardware that ended up being the bottleneck rather than the enabler.

So my general heuristic is this: buy whatever is commoditized and good enough, so you can start collecting data and learning tomorrow instead of next year. Build when the off-the-shelf option fundamentally caps what your system can learn, or when owning it lets you iterate in a way nobody else can. And revisit the decision often, because the landscape is moving incredibly fast. Things that weren't buyable two years ago, like decent low-cost arms, teleoperation rigs, and even humanoid platforms, are now available. What was a necessary build yesterday might be a distraction today.

The last thing I'd add is to think about the co-design question. In the long run, the hardware and the learning system probably should be designed together. The data you can collect is shaped by the embodiment, and the embodiment should be shaped by what's learnable. So even if you buy early, keep a path open to vertical integration once you know what really matters. Just don't pay that cost before you've earned the knowledge to do it right.

r001.rationale: The response recommends buying commoditized components, but says teams should build parts of the learning loop and may need custom hardware. It does not state that a team can buy all components if its integration is sufficiently deep.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the buy-or-build question in robotics is really a question about where you think your edge is going to come from, and most teams get it wrong by answering it as a cost question instead.

Let me unpack that a bit. If you're a team chasing something like physical AGI, your scarce resource is not money and it's not even talent, it's the rate at which you can learn from the physical world. Every decision should be filtered through: does this increase my iteration speed with real robots and real data, or does it slow it down?

With that lens, hardware is mostly a buy. There was a period, maybe five or six years ago, where you almost had to build your own platform because nothing off the shelf was reliable enough to run thousands of episodes. That's largely changed. You can buy arms, hands, mobile bases, even full humanoids now, that are good enough to collect data at scale. If you spend eighteen months designing a custom actuator before you've collected a single trajectory, you've probably lost. The exception is when the form factor itself is your hypothesis, say you believe a particular hand design unlocks a class of manipulation nobody else can do. Then that's not infrastructure, that's the research, and you should build it.

Software is where it gets more subtle. The temptation in academia and in startups is to rebuild everything: your own simulator, your own data pipeline, your own training stack. I've been guilty of this. My rule now is that you build the parts that touch your core bet and you buy or borrow everything else. If your bet is that a particular data representation or a particular way of mixing simulation with real data is the key, then you own that layer completely, you need to be able to tear it apart on a Tuesday afternoon. But the robot drivers, the logging, the experiment tracking, the base model you fine-tune from, those should be commodities. Nobody is going to get to physical AGI because they wrote a better ROS wrapper.

Foundation models are the hardest call right now. Do you train your own vision-language-action model from scratch or start from someone else's? My view is that for almost everyone, starting from a strong pretrained model is right, because the thing that differentiates you is the embodied data and the post-training recipe, not the language and vision pretraining. But you need to be clear-eyed that you're inheriting someone else's inductive biases and someone else's roadmap. If the model provider changes direction, you're exposed. So I'd say buy, but keep enough internal capability that you could build if you had to. That optionality is worth paying for.

And one more thing. People treat this as a one-time decision and it isn't. The right answer flips as the field matures. Something you had to build in 2023 is a commodity in 2026, and something that looks like a commodity today might become the differentiator once everyone has the same base models. So revisit it every six months or so and be willing to throw away things you built with a lot of love. That's painful, but holding onto infrastructure out of sunk cost is one of the quietest ways a robotics team dies.

r001.rationale: The response recommends buying many components, but says teams should build hardware when the form factor is their research hypothesis and own software layers tied to their core bet. It does not state that all components can be bought if integration is sufficiently deep.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking: what is the core hypothesis your team is trying to prove? Physical AGI is a very broad goal, and you can easily end up trying to build everything—the hardware, the simulation, the data infrastructure, the learning algorithms. Then it becomes very difficult to learn which part is actually holding you back.

If your hypothesis is about learning generalizable behaviors, I would buy a reasonably capable robot and use existing infrastructure wherever possible. Put your effort into the learning system and the data loop. But if existing hardware fundamentally prevents you from collecting the right experience or performing the tasks you care about, then building hardware might be necessary.

The important thing is to keep that decision tied to experiments. What can you buy that lets you test your idea sooner? What do you need to own because it determines how quickly you can improve? I wouldn’t treat buying as giving up an advantage, or building as automatically creating one. Build where you have a clear reason to believe your approach needs something different, and let that boundary change as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response recommends buying a capable robot and existing infrastructure in some cases, but it does not say the team can buy all components if its integration is sufficiently deep.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with: what is the core hypothesis your team is trying to prove? If you’re trying to build general-purpose robot intelligence, you probably don’t want to spend all your time reinventing motors, robot arms, or basic infrastructure. Buy what lets you get to the learning problem faster.

But you have to own the parts that determine whether your hypothesis works. That might be the data collection pipeline, the learning system, or the connection between the policy and the hardware. If an off-the-shelf component prevents you from collecting the right data or running the experiments you need, then building becomes worthwhile.

So I wouldn’t make it an ideological decision. Start with what’s available, find the actual bottleneck, and build there. The important thing is how quickly your team can go through the cycle of collecting data, training, deploying, and learning from failures.

r001.rationale: The response recommends buying some components and building parts that determine whether the hypothesis works, but it does not state that all components can be bought if integration is sufficiently deep.
